Regarding the term "mirror-sun-jewel" (*jing ri zhu*): "mirror" (*jing*) refers to what Nāgārjuna (Longshu) of antiquity called it; "sun-jewel" (*ri zhu*) refers to what Aśvaghoṣa (Maming) of antiquity called it.
It is said that during the time when Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world, there was an elder named Cakragandha who had a daughter named Maṇitīrtha. As it is like this...
These two individuals each offered the seven treasures to Kāśyapa Buddha and requested him to grant them offspring. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the two, saying:
"Go quickly and return to your respective places; seventeen days from now, what you have requested shall be accomplished and your wishes fulfilled.
Then the two bowed their heads to the ground in prostration before the Buddha and returned to their original locations. (Chapter Seventeen)
On that day, when all [the preparations] were fully completed, the woman from the jeweled pond had an auspicious dream in which she experienced great joy beyond compare.
Specifically, she dreamed: first, a radiant discus of the sun came and entered her womb;
second, a brilliant, full moon discus came and entered her womb. Having experienced these auspicious omens for nine months, she then gave birth to two [sons].
The elder brother was named Sun-Jewel (Sūryamaṇi) and the younger brother was named Moon-Mirror (Candramukha); they were given these names according to their respective physical characteristics.

When these two sons reached the age of seven, they immediately left the household life and went to the Buddha Kāśyapa. Following the World-Honored One, they cultivated his Dharma and practice, constantly making this vow:
"In birth after birth and in every place, may we not be separated from one another; as companions in study, may we establish the Right [Dharma]."
Because these two Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with the Dharma, sublime conduct, mindfulness, and the ocean of awakening, they do not abandon one another;
they proceed and revolve together, manifesting their original liberation to benefit sentient beings.

Now, the author of this introduction takes the name from that time to establish the title, referring to them as "Moon-Mirror" and "Sun-Jewel. For what reason does he omit their current names and take those of the past?

The titles of the two treatises, *Mūlamadhyamaka* and *Prasannapadā*, remove the darkness of ignorance and increase the light of wisdom. For sentient beings who are blind and in the dark, they are able to provide illumination and clarity.
Just as the two luminaries both produce light to dispel the night and guide sentient beings so that they are not troubled or disturbed, the circumstances and the timing coincide;
thus, the title "Madhyamaka" (the Middle Way) was established for it, and this is all there is to it regarding such causes and conditions.
In the third fascicle of the *Aśvaghoṣa-bodhisattva-pūrvayoga-nidāna-śāstra*, it states that "Light" (Āloka) is the name of the Tathāgata from a former age who was Aśvaghoṣa,
and "Wondrous Cloud" (Sudharmamegha) is the name of the Tathāgata from a former age who was Nāgārjuna.
These two names are each explained differently within the sūtras as referring to Vajrasamyagjñāna (Vajra Right Wisdom).
In the sutras it is stated thus: for the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, [the Buddha was] Mahāprabhāsa; for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, [the Buddha was] Meghasvararāja.
In the *Mahāvyūha-samādhi-sūtra* it is stated thus: for the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, [the Buddha was] Samantāvabhāsānugata-ananta-tathāgata;
for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, [the Buddha was] Samantavyūha-prathamotpāda-tathāgata, according to the *Gambhīra-maṇḍala-sūtra*.
In the middle, it is stated as follows: "The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa says that the Tathāgata Sun-Moon-Star Brilliance now relies upon the *Vajrasamyagjñāna-sūtra*.
The master of the preface states that [this refers to] the 'Radiant Wondrous Cloud Aspect' (*Prabhāsvara-megha-lakṣaṇa*).

The phrase "separated by the gate of dāna" refers to entering the direct gate of the *Yìrúizàng* (Wish-Fulfilling Treasury); the phrase "proceeding toward the stage" refers to entering the sūtra-gate of the *Yìrúizàng*.

The term *vimalacakkhu* (translated here as "pure eye") is a metaphorical name; it refers to the "pupil" (*cakkhu*) within the eye.
It is exceedingly minute—comparable, for example, to a speck of dust on a rabbit's fur—and its dimensions are without variation.
Yet, it is capable of receiving and perceiving the colors of light and darkness filling the ten directions. The general meaning of this treatise is likewise so; therefore, it is titled *Tālapuṭa*.
This "cloud-gas thread" (yunqi si) is precisely the "dragon-thread" (longsi);

it refers to what is called the single gas-thread within the tongue of a dragon king, which is exceedingly subtle—its measure being no different from that of a hair—and yet is capable of producing and absorbing various dense clouds that fill the ten directions.
The general purport of this treatise is likewise thus; for this reason, the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa manifested [himself] during the six periods.
When was the treatise on the teaching of conditioned origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) composed? It was composed when [the Buddha] had appeared for over one hundred years.
What are the four precious volumes of this treatise? First, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Arousing of Faith); second, the *Mysterious Principle Treatise* (*Xuanli lun*);

third, the *Fundamental Origin Treatise* (*Benyuan lun*); and fourth, the *Purity Treatise* (*Qingjing lun*). It was composed during the period when [the Buddha] had appeared for over three hundred years.
He composed the *Ṣaṭpāda-śāstra* (Treatise in Six Sections). What are the six? First, the *Samādhi-śāstra*;
second, the *Ekībhāva-śāstra*; third, the *Sūkṣma-śāstra*; fourth, the *Madhyagarbha-śāstra*; fifth, the *Pratyāgata-tattva-śāstra*; and sixth, the *Vyāpti-śāstra*.

During his six hundredth year, he produced twenty treatises, including the *Mārgapraveśa-śāstra* (Treatise on Entering the Path), which served as an antidote to heterodox knowledge, all written in elegant Chinese prose. (From the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*)

The Treatises on Manifestation (*Changde Sanmei Jing*): During the period of eight hundred years [after the Buddha’s passing], thirty treatises in Chinese script were produced, including the *Mahā-samaya-śāstra*.

The Treatises on the Manifestation of the Flower-Writing (*Dacheng Benfa Lun*): At the time when the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, forty treatises in Chinese script were produced, including the *Sāṃghāṭī-karmāvaraṇa-mahāsāgara-śāstra*.

For example, when a bird flies through the void at the moment it crosses a brilliant light, ten kinds of harmonious sounds are produced; the *ākāśa-cakra-akṣara* (the wheel-syllable of space) should be contemplated in this manner.
As for what are called the "ten sounds," they refer to the ten subtle particles (*paramāṇu*) coming into contact with one another at the single moment the bird crosses the brilliant light.
Because subtle sounds emerge, one takes up a single sound from each of those particles; therefore, it is said that ten kinds of harmonious sounds emerge.
